decisions.decision: Launch PolicyServer as a genuine OS subprocess (subprocess.Popen), not a threading.Thread inside the notebook kernel.
decisions.rationale: A crash inside a background thread in the SAME process as the Jupyter/Colab kernel silently kills the ENTIRE kernel with zero traceback ('Kernel crashed' only) -- confirmed this was exactly what happened on every prior Test 7 attempt. A separate subprocess isolates the blast radius and gives a real, file-backed log that survives even a hard native crash.

decisions.decision: Give Fast-FoundationStereo's torch/cuDNN install (Step 7) its own fully isolated Python environment, never touching the shared site-packages PolicyServer's subprocess reads from.
decisions.rationale: ROOT CAUSE, confirmed via exact policy_server.log timeline correlation + `pip show torch nvidia-cudnn-cu12` diagnostic + `policy_server_process.poll()` returning -6 (SIGABRT): cuDNN 9.x splits into plugin .so files (libcudnn_graph.so, etc.) that PyTorch dlopen's LAZILY on first real use, not at import time. Step 7's `pip install torch==2.6.0 ... cu124` overwrites the shared on-disk cuDNN files WHILE PolicyServer's subprocess is already running and hasn't yet lazy-loaded that plugin. When it finally does (at the very first real inference call), it loads the NEW, mismatched file and hits an unresolved symbol -- a native, uncatchable abort. Process-level isolation (the subprocess fix above) does NOT protect against this on its own, since both processes still share one filesystem.

decisions.decision: Use `virtualenv` (pip-installed) for Fast-FoundationStereo's isolated environment, NOT the stdlib `venv` module.
decisions.rationale: First attempt using `venv` + `apt-get install python3-venv` FAILED live: Colab's OS-level `apt` `python3` alias resolves to 3.10, while the actual active interpreter is 3.12 -- apt tried to fetch the wrong package (`python3.10-venv`), which 404'd from the Ubuntu mirror, leaving `venv`'s bundled `ensurepip` broken ('No module named pip'). `virtualenv` bundles its own pip/setuptools/wheel and needs no OS package at all, so this class of failure can't recur.

decisions.decision: Set KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK=TRUE / OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 globally and in both the PolicyServer and FastFS subprocess environments.
decisions.rationale: Defensive guard against Colab's classic duplicate-OpenMP-runtime crash (OMP: Error #15), which manifests identically to what was initially observed (abrupt, tracebackless kernel death right as a new library's compute path first runs). Note: the ACTUAL root cause found tonight was the cuDNN lazy-load race above, not confirmed to be an OMP conflict -- this guard remains a reasonable defensive addition, not the fix that resolved the crash.

decisions.decision: For tonight's retry, skip depth capture entirely (omit --depth-endpoint/--depth-calibration) rather than live-patch depth_client.compute_depth() into an async call.
decisions.rationale: The synchronous-blocking design has dedicated existing test coverage (test_run_vla_episode.py, test_depth_camera.py per 12-06-SUMMARY.md) asserting synchronous, exactly-once-per-tick behavior. Changing it live, without running/updating that suite, risks a new bug in safety-critical control-loop code while actively testing on real hardware. This is a workaround to validate the crash fix in isolation, NOT a fix for Test 7's actual pass criteria.

decisions.decision: GPU tier: L4 is sufficient; explicitly do NOT move to A100 to fix the depth latency.
decisions.rationale: Confirmed via `torch.cuda.is_available()` returning True with 'NVIDIA L4' correctly reported inside the fastfs_venv -- ruling out CPU-fallback. The 15-70s/call latency is dominated by process-spawn + torch/cv2 re-import + full model-checkpoint-reload-from-disk overhead on EVERY single request (Step 8's subprocess.run()-per-call design, zero model persistence), not GPU compute -- the actual inference step is fast (sub-second) once a model is loaded. A faster GPU only speeds up the already-fast part. The real fix is a persistent, model-resident depth server (same pattern PolicyServer already uses), not more powerful hardware.
